1.title: Issues, Projects and Team Habits
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: Issues, Projects and Team Habits. It covers the exam area Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Use issues, labels, assignees, milestones and templates. Use project boards and Discussions. Write good commit messages. Install a commit-msg hook. Keep P Rs small and review well. Write a contributing file. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.text: Here is where this module sits in the course. Part: Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Verified with: Git two point five zero.one for the local parts; the Git Hub documentation (read twenty twenty-six-eleven to sixteen) for the Git Hub parts.

1.text: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only. Every Git command in this module was run for real in practice repositories. The Git Hub features come from the official Git Hub documentation or general practice and were not run.

1.title: Issues, projects and Discussions
1.text: Issues, projects and Discussions. Teams stay in step when work is visible. An issue tracks one bug, task or question. A good issue has a title that names the problem, the steps to reproduce it, and what you expected instead.

1.title: Issues, projects and Discussions, continued
1.text: Issues, projects and Discussions. The figure shows this: Team habits around a repository: issues feed branches and pull requests, commit messages and small P Rs keep history readable, and blame, log and bisect explain it later.

1.title: Issues, projects and Discussions, continued
1.text: Issues, projects and Discussions. Labels. Categories such as bug, docs or an area of the code; you filter by them. Assignees. The person who owns the work. Milestones. A group of issues for one release or date. Templates. A form of questions that every new issue starts from.

1.title: Issues, projects and Discussions, continued
1.text: Issues, projects and Discussions. A P R that says Closes hash forty-two closes the issue when it merges into the default branch (module nine). A project board lays out issues and P Rs by status, so everyone sees what is waiting, in progress or done. Discussions hold open questions and ideas that are not tasks yet. When a discussion turns into work, open an issue. Tip: One issue, one outcome. If an issue needs "and also" in its title, split it, so each P R can close exactly one issue.

1.title: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook
1.text: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook. History is read far more often than it is written, so write for the reader six months from now. Subject. About fifty characters, imperative ("Add", "Fix"), no final period. Blank line. Always separates the subject from the body. Body. Wrapped at about seventy-two characters; explain why, because the diff shows what. Footer. References such as Closes hash forty-two.

1.title: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook, continued
1.text: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook. Conventional Commits add a type to the subject: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test or chore, optionally with a scope, as in fix cart round the total. Try it. Write a commit with a subject, a body and a footer, then read it back. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook, continued
1.text: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook. A commit-msg hook is a script that Git runs after you write the message. It receives the path of the message file, and a non-zero exit cancels the commit. Git hooks live in dot git slash hooks, which is not cloned. Keep the script in a tracked folder such as dot githooks, mark it executable in the index with git update index the chmod flag set to plus x, and let each clone run git config core dot hooks Path dot githooks once. Try it. This hook allows only the six types and at most seventy-two characters, and lets merge and revert messages through.

1.title: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook, continued
1.text: Good commit messages and a commit-msg hook. No commit is made. Tested here: a good subject is accepted, a subject over seventy-two characters is rejected, and a fresh clone has no hook until core dot hooks Path is set. git commit the no verify flag skips the hook, so a hook helps but does not enforce: the real gate is a server-side check. Tip: Explain why in the body, not what. Anyone can read the diff, but only you know the reason for the change.

1.title: Small pull requests and review etiquette
1.text: Small pull requests and review etiquette. A small P R has one purpose and can be read in minutes. It gets faster and better reviews, is easier to test, and is easier to undo. If the description needs "and also", split it. A reviewer checks, in this order. Does the change do what the description and the issue say? Is it correct, tested and readable, and do the checks succeed? Does it touch anything it should not, such as unrelated files, secrets or large files?

1.title: Small pull requests and review etiquette, continued
1.text: Small pull requests and review etiquette. Write comments about the code, not the person. Ask a question rather than give an order. Say why, and suggest an alternative. Mark a minor taste as optional, for instance with "nit:". Say what is good too. Use Request changes only for real blockers, and Approve when the rest is minor. Authors answer every comment and push fixes as new commits. A contributing.md file in the repository tells newcomers how to propose changes: branch names, commit style, how to run the tests and what review to expect.

1.title: Small pull requests and review etiquette, continued
1.text: Small pull requests and review etiquette. Large files make every clone slower, because Git keeps every version of every file. Git L F S (Large File Storage) stores small pointer files in the repository and the real content on a separate server. You pick files with git lfs track and commit the dot gitattributes file it writes. The course does not run it. Tip: Split a P R that cannot be reviewed in one sitting. Smaller changes get faster and better reviews.

1.title: Debugging history as a team
1.text: Debugging history as a team. Three commands answer "who, when and which commit". git blame dash L three,four file shows who last changed lines three to four. git log dash S text lists commits that added or removed that text. git bisect run finds the first bad commit by binary search with a test script. Try it. Blame two lines, then search for the text that was removed. Your hashes and dates will differ.

2.text: Debugging history as a team. Blame shows who last touched a line, not who caused the bug, so read the commit. The dash S search found both the commit that added rate twenty and the one that removed it. Try it. test dot sh fails on the newest commit. Mark the bad and the good commit, and let Git search.

2.title: Debugging history as a team, continued
2.text: Debugging history as a team. The test script must exist at every commit that bisect checks out, or live outside the repository. It exits zero for good and non-zero, such as one, for bad. Exit code one hundred twenty-five means "skip this commit": if the neighbor of the bad commit is skipped, bisect lists both commits as suspects. Finish with git bisect reset. Tip: Write the failing test first, then run git bisect run. A script that exits zero or one turns hours of guessing into a few automatic steps.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A teammate asks which subject line follows the team habits. Which one is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: fix: round the cart total half up. It has a known type, an imperative summary, a short length and no final period.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Ada's commit-msg hook rejects bad subjects, but Bob's fresh clone accepts them. What is the cause and the fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: dot git slash hooks is not cloned; commit a hooks folder and set core dot hooks Path. The hooks folder is local to each clone, so the team shares a tracked folder and points Git at it.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. git blame dash L three,four total dot sh shows line three as c f three eight one three f seven bob three rate two. What does that tell you? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Bob's commit last changed line three, so read that commit next. Blame names the last commit to touch a line, which is a lead, not a verdict.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. You need every commit that added or removed the text rate twenty. Which command does that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: git log dash S rate twenty, which finds commits that change the text. The dash S search finds commits where the number of occurrences of the text changes.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A P R changes one thousand eight hundred lines across three unrelated features, and the checks are green. What is the best review response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Ask the author to split it into small single-purpose P Rs. Small, single-purpose P Rs get better reviews and are easy to revert.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Designers commit large source files, and every clone slows down. What helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Track the files with Git L F S so the repo holds small pointers. L F S keeps pointer files in the repository and the large content on a separate server.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What are the usual limits for the subject and the body of a commit message? Answer: About fifty characters for the subject and about seventy-two characters per body line. Question two. Which six Conventional Commits types does this course use? Answer: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test and chore. Question three. How does a team share a commit-msg hook? Answer: Commit it in a folder such as dot githooks, and run git config core dot hooks Path dot githooks in each clone.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which command shows who last changed lines three and four of a file? Answer: git blame dash L three,four file. Question five. What do the exit codes of a git bisect run script mean? Answer: zero is good, a non-zero code such as one is bad, and one hundred twenty-five skips the commit. Question six. Which option skips a commit-msg hook? Answer: git commit the no verify flag.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Issues: labels, assignees, milestones, templates; one issue, one outcome. Boards and Discussions: boards show status; Discussions hold open questions and ideas. Commit message: subject about fifty characters, imperative; blank line; body about seventy-two, explains why. Conventional Commits: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore. commit-msg hook: non-zero exit cancels the commit; not cloned; use core dot hooks Path; the no verify flag skips. Small P Rs: one purpose; reviewer checks intent, correctness and side effects. Review comments: about the code; question, reason, alternative; optional for taste. Large files: Git L F S keeps pointers in the repository, content elsewhere. Debugging history: git blame dash L, git log dash S, git bisect run with exit zero, one or one hundred twenty-five.
